title: Why 2D Models Fail to Capture Flow Properties in 3D Heterogeneous Media: A Connectivity Perspective
authors: Cristian Picighelli, Ivan Colecchio, Marcelo Piva, Alejandro D. Otero, Alejandro Boschan
abstract: We analyze how the equivalent hydraulic conductivity, $K_{eq}$, varies with the coarsening scale $λ/I$ in 2D and 3D heterogeneous media. Their local hydraulic conductivity, $k({\bf r})$, follows a lognormal distribution in all cases, while spatial connectivity of $k({\bf r})$ ranges from high (HCS), through intermediate or multi-Gaussian (ICS) and low (LCS), to unstructured (NS). Using a stochastic approach, we characterize the full distribution $P[\log(K_{eq})]$, and its moments: mean $\langle K_{eq}\rangle$, log-variance $σ_{\log(K_{eq})}^{2}$, and log-skewness $γ_{\log(K_{eq})}$, as a function of $λ/I$. Significant contrasts appear between 2D and 3D, which we interpret in terms of two key factors associated with spatial dimensionality. We observe that, compared with ICS, LCS and HCS exhibit two distinct features: existing analytical expressions for coarse-graining of $k({\bf r})$ in multi-Gaussian media do not apply, while $P[\log(K_{eq})]$ deviates from Gaussian at all scales $λ/I$. Critical path analysis is then used to quantify the connectivity of our samples, and show that $K_{eq}$ exhibits a power-law dependence on it. Our results reveal that connectivity can lead to substantial differences between 2D and 3D macroscopic flow properties, even for the same geostatistical parameters, highlighting the severe limitations of using 2D models to represent 3D flows.
summary: This work analyzes how flow properties in heterogeneous media are determined by spatial dimensionality and connectivity. By comparing 2D and 3D models, the authors demonstrate that 2D approximations fail to capture the true physics of 3D flow, especially when connectivity constraints are factored in. The study uses stochastic methods to quantify these critical differences in effective conductivity.
main_problem: The paper investigates why simplified 2D models fail to accurately predict macroscopic flow properties when applied to complex, heterogeneous 3D media.
main_result: Significant differences exist between 2D and 3D flow properties, particularly when connectivity is considered, demonstrating that 2D models severely underestimate the complexity of 3D flow.
method: The authors use a stochastic approach, analyzing the upscaling of equivalent hydraulic conductivity ($K_{eq}$) across various connectivity structures (HCS, ICS, LCS) in both 2D and 3D realizations.
model_or_system: The system is flow through heterogeneous porous media, governed by Laplace's equation, where the local hydraulic conductivity $k(\mathbf{r})$ is modeled as a lognormal random field.
key_observables: Equivalent hydraulic conductivity ($K_{eq}$), the full distribution $P[\log(K_{eq})]$, and its moments (mean, log-variance, log-skewness).
important_parameters: Coarsening scale ($\lambda$) relative to the integral scale ($I$), and the spatial dimensionality ($D=2$ vs $D=3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on characterizing the flow behavior across different connectivity regimes (HCS, ICS, LCS) and comparing the mathematical validity of 2D vs 3D upscaling formulas.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spatial maps of conductivity realizations and show quantitative comparisons of $K_{eq}$ and its distribution moments across different connectivity types and dimensions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the upscaling of $K_{eq}$ in 2D and 3D media, contrasting the behavior of different connectivity structures (HCS, ICS, LCS) and highlighting the mathematical and physical divergences between the two dimensions.
why_interesting: While focused on fluid dynamics, the core methodology—analyzing how dimensionality and connectivity constrain macroscopic properties from microscopic disorder—shares conceptual parallels with understanding emergent behavior in complex, disordered quantum systems.

Figure 3: Hydraulic conductivity maps of Y = log[k(r)] showing the different connectivity structures of the 3D media samples of linear size L = 256∆. Here (a) NS, (b) ICS, (c) HCS, and (d) LCS. Maps are shown for fine log-variance σ2 Y = 2.
Figure 4: Probability density function P[log(Keq)] of (a–c) 2D, and (d–f) 3D media samples for (a, d) HCS, (b, e) ICS, and (c, f) LCS, with σ2 Y = 2 in all cases.

Log-variances: σ2 Y = 0.5 (△), σ2 Y = 1 (⃝), and σ2 Y = 2 (□). Dashed lines ( ) in (b) and (e) show the analytical results of Eq. 4, with as = 1.3 for both 2D and 3D. The symbols (×) and (+), in (a–c) and in (d–f), respectively, show the numerical results from Zinn and Harvey (2003) (2D), and those from Jankovic et al. (2017) (3D), for σ2 Y = 2.
